lessons.title: Sorting the Candy Jar
lessons.content_md:
# The Magnifying Glass 🔍

Imagine you are given a gigantic jar filled with 10,000 mixed candies: M&Ms, Skittles, jellybeans, and gummies. They are all mixed together in a chaotic pile.

If someone asks you, *"Are there more red M&Ms or green Skittles?"*, you can't just stare at the jar and guess. You have to take action.

You dump the jar on the table and start **sorting**.

First, you group all the M&Ms together. Then, you filter out all the colors except red. Then you do the same for the green Skittles. Finally, you count them and compare.

## The Power of Aggregation

Data Scientists do this exact same thing, but instead of candies, they use data.

When faced with a massive dataset of 5 million store purchases, the data is too messy to read line by line. So, the Data Scientist uses code to:
1. **Filter:** Throw away any data that isn't from the year 2024.
2. **Group:** Put all the clothing purchases in one bucket, and all the electronics purchases in another bucket.
3. **Aggregate:** Calculate the total sum of money spent in each bucket.

<flipcard front="🧹 What does it mean to Filter data?" back="To remove rows of data that you don't care about, so you can focus only on what's relevant to your investigation."></flipcard>

<flipcard front="🪣 What does it mean to Group data?" back="To sort data into distinct categories or 'buckets' based on a specific shared trait (like grouping users by country)."></flipcard>

<flipcard front="➕ What is Aggregation?" back="Performing math on a group of data to get a single summary number, like taking the Average, Sum, or Maximum of a group."></flipcard>
